planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in a shaded, humid site with loose, humus-rich, fast-draining soil; this small Vietnamese forest-floor cycad scorches quickly in direct sun and needs steady warmth to establish.

directions: Site this dwarf Vietnamese species in dappled or bright shade with consistent moisture and rich, leafy soil, since it comes from the humid limestone forest floor of northern Vietnam rather than open, sun-baked ground. Its trunk stays low and often decumbent, while each frond splits into narrow, twice-divided (bipinnate) segments that give the whole plant a delicate, fern-like texture quite unlike the coarse, stiff foliage of most cycads. It is markedly smaller and more compact in every dimension than the similarly bipinnate Cycas debaoensis, making it a better fit for shaded understory beds or large containers than open beds. Keep it away from hard frost and prolonged cold, wet soil, both of which quickly rot the shallow root system.

planting.note: Plant in full sun in lean, sandy, fast-draining soil; this fire-adapted grassland cycad from mainland Southeast Asia is one of the most drought- and heat-tolerant Cycas species and resents rich, wet ground.

directions: Cycas siamensis grows across the seasonally dry savannas and open dipterocarp woodlands of Thailand, Myanmar, Laos, and Cambodia, where its thick trunk typically stays buried underground or barely emerges above the soil line even in old plants. Stiff, gray-green to blue-green leaflets are held in a low, symmetrical crown that survives annual dry-season fires in the wild, so it tolerates neglect and poor, sandy soils far better than most cultivated cycads. It stays noticeably shorter and squatter than Cycas revoluta or Cycas circinalis, making it useful as a tough, sculptural low accent in rock gardens and xeriscape beds. Give it excellent drainage and reserve supplemental water for only the driest stretches once established.
sources: Kew Science — Plants of the World Online: Cycas siamensis

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in partial shade to full sun in deep, humus-rich, well-drained soil; this is one of the larger-growing Cycas species and appreciates more moisture and richer soil than the drought-adapted species in the genus.

directions: Native to the foothills of the eastern Himalaya, from northeastern India and Bangladesh through Yunnan into Indochina, Cycas pectinata builds a stout, eventually tall trunk topped with long, glossy dark-green pinnate fronds arranged in a dense crown. It grows in monsoon-influenced forests with a pronounced wet season, so it wants considerably more regular moisture through the growing season than desert or savanna cycads and will not thrive on a strict xeric regimen. Local communities in its native range have long processed the toxic seeds into food after extensive leaching, but the raw seed and all other plant parts remain poisonous and should never be eaten. In cultivation it rewards patience with one of the more substantial, tree-like silhouettes among cultivated Cycas species.
sources: Kew Science — Plants of the World Online: Cycas pectinata

planting.note: Plant in full sun in lean, rocky, fast-draining soil; this north Queensland species is one of the most drought-tolerant and heat-loving cycads and needs excellent drainage to avoid crown rot.

directions: Cycas cairnsiana comes from rocky, exposed hillsides near Mareeba in far north Queensland, Australia, one of the hottest and driest habitats of any cycad in the genus. Its leaflets emerge with a striking powder-blue to silvery-gray cast that intensifies in full sun, giving it a color and texture closer to the blue Encephalartos species than to the typical glossy green Cycas. The trunk stays short and often subterranean in younger plants, keeping the whole specimen compact and low relative to species like Cycas circinalis or Cycas rumphii. It is an outstanding accent for hot, sun-drenched xeriscape and gravel gardens where its silvery color reads as a deliberate contrast plant.
sources: Kew Science — Plants of the World Online: Cycas cairnsiana

planting.note: Plant in full sun to light shade in gritty, well-drained limestone-based soil; like its Sichuan relative Cycas panzhihuaensis, this species handles brief winter chill better than most tropical cycads.

directions: Cycas guizhouensis is a limestone-adapted species from the karst hills of Guizhou Province in southern China, where it experiences cool, occasionally frosty winters unlike most Cycas habitats. It develops a short, thick, often subterranean stem with a crown of stiff, deep-green leaflets that hold up well against seasonal drought on shallow rocky soils. Its cold tolerance sits between the very hardy Cycas panzhihuaensis and the strictly tropical species like Cycas rumphii, making it a reasonable candidate for gardeners at the cooler edge of cycad-growing country who want insurance against an occasional light freeze. Grow it on a raised, gritty mound to replicate the sharp drainage of its native limestone outcrops.
sources: Kew Science — Plants of the World Online: Cycas guizhouensis

planting.note: Plant container stock or rooted offsets in spring in deep, bright shade with rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil; this rainforest-floor species has no cold tolerance and needs shelter from direct sun and any chill below the mid-40s F.

directions: Zamia skinneri grows on the shaded floor of lowland rainforest in Panama and Costa Rica, forming a subterranean or barely emergent stem topped by a handful of broad, deeply veined, glossy dark-green leaflets that are markedly wider than those of Zamia furfuracea or Zamia integrifolia. It reproduces readily by suckering offsets at the base, so established clumps can be divided rather than waiting on the slow seed cycle. Because it never develops a visible trunk and stays low and spreading, it works well as a bold-textured groundcover under a shaded, humid canopy where showier cycads would burn. It has no frost tolerance whatsoever and needs to be lifted or covered well ahead of any cold snap outside the deep tropics.

planting.note: Mount offsets or container plants on a well-drained epiphyte basket or tree fern fiber in bright shade with high humidity; do not plant directly in dense garden soil, since this species naturally roots in the loose organic debris that collects in the crooks of rainforest trees.

directions: Zamia pseudoparasitica is the only cycad species in the world known to grow naturally as a true epiphyte, rooting high in the branches and mossy crotches of large trees in the cloud forests of central Panama rather than in the ground. Its long, pendulous fronds hang downward from the perch point, a growth habit unlike any terrestrial Zamia and one that gives the species its odd 'false parasite' epithet, even though it takes no nourishment from its host tree. Because it depends on constant humidity and free-draining organic debris rather than garden soil, it is best grown mounted in a hanging basket or on a slab with orchid-style bark mix, watered and misted like a large epiphytic fern. It is a genuine specialist collector's plant, propagated in cultivation from offsets and seed by a small number of botanical gardens and cycad enthusiasts.
sources: Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute — Panama cycads

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in partial shade in well-drained, humus-rich soil; this small Veracruz cycad suits pots and border edges where a compact, patterned-leaf accent is wanted.

directions: Zamia fischeri is a diminutive cycad from the humid forests of Veracruz, Mexico, staying under two feet tall with a mostly subterranean caudex that keeps it noticeably smaller than the closely related Zamia loddigesii or Zamia purpurea. Its narrow, dark-green leaflets are often lightly mottled or flecked, giving the foliage a subtly patterned look that stands out at close range in a shaded border or container grouping. Being one of the smallest cultivated Zamia species, it is well suited to raised beds, rock gardens, and pots where larger cycads would be out of scale. Protect it from standing water and hard freezes, though it tolerates brief light cold better than strictly tropical Zamia species.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in bright, filtered shade in fast-draining, humus-rich soil; new flushes of leaves need protection from strong midday sun to keep their purple color from bleaching green too quickly.

directions: Zamia purpurea, native to seasonally dry tropical forest in the Mexican state of Guerrero, is grown chiefly for its emerging fronds, which unfurl in shades of deep burgundy to plum-purple before gradually maturing to green over several weeks. This color change is far more pronounced than in any other cultivated Zamia species and makes fresh growth flushes a seasonal highlight rather than an incidental feature. The plant stays compact and stemless to nearly stemless, with a low rosette habit similar in scale to Zamia fischeri but distinguished immediately by its colored new leaves. Give it a sheltered, part-shaded spot to preserve the purple flush and protect it from any frost, since it has essentially no cold hardiness.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun to light shade in sandy, well-drained soil; this species is more sun-tolerant than most forest-floor Zamia and adapts well to open beds.

directions: First described in the early nineteenth century and named for the Loddiges nursery of London, Zamia loddigesii is native to the coastal plains of Veracruz and Tamaulipas, Mexico, where it grows in open savanna and scrub rather than deep forest shade. Its subterranean caudex sends up narrow, slightly glossy leaflets on a moderate number of fronds, giving it a leaner, more open crown than the broad-leaved Zamia skinneri. Because its native habitat is seasonally dry, open grassland, it tolerates considerably more direct sun and drought than most other cultivated Zamia species. It is a good choice for a sunnier cycad bed where the shade-loving species in this dataset would struggle.
sources: Kew Science — Plants of the World Online: Zamia loddigesii

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun to light shade in well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic soil in zone 9b–11; this coastal species tolerates more moisture and salt exposure than most Encephalartos.

directions: Encephalartos ferox grows along the coastal dune forests and grasslands of KwaZulu-Natal and Mozambique, staying low and often nearly stemless for many years before slowly forming a short, thick trunk. Its dark, glossy leaflets have sharply spined, wavy margins that give the species its 'ferocious' epithet, and mature cones emerge in vivid orange to scarlet, among the showiest cone displays in the genus. Unlike the strictly xeric Encephalartos horridus or E. lehmannii, this coastal species handles higher humidity, sandier soil, and occasional salt spray, making it a strong choice for Gulf Coast gardens closer to the shoreline. Full sun brings out the deepest leaf color, though it also performs well with light shade in hotter inland gardens.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun on lean, gritty, fast-draining soil in zone 9–11; this arid Eastern Cape species is extremely intolerant of wet, heavy soil and needs a raised, sharply drained planting site.

directions: Encephalartos horridus is a low, suckering cycad from the semi-arid valley bushveld of the Eastern Cape, prized above nearly every other Encephalartos species for the intense steel-blue to silver-blue color of its stiffly recurved, deeply twisted, heavily spined leaflets. It stays compact and often clump-forming, rarely developing much of a visible trunk, which keeps its scale distinctly smaller than tall species like Encephalartos transvenosus or E. natalensis. The dramatic, almost sculptural leaf form and unmistakable blue coloring make single specimens effective as a focal accent in dry, sun-drenched rock or succulent plantings. It demands sharp drainage and minimal summer water, since its native habitat is thorny, rocky scrub with low, erratic rainfall.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in partial shade to full sun in deep, well-drained, humus-enriched soil in zone 9–11; this is one of the larger, faster-growing Encephalartos species and rewards richer soil than the dry-country species in the genus.

directions: Encephalartos natalensis is native to the forest margins, grassland, and rocky slopes of KwaZulu-Natal and the Eastern Cape, where it forms one of the largest and most robust trunks in the genus, eventually reaching tree-like proportions over many decades. Long, arching, glossy dark-green fronds create a full, tropical-looking crown that is fuller and denser than the stiffer, more upright foliage of E. ferox or E. horridus. It grows faster and tolerates richer, moister soil better than most Encephalartos species, making it one of the more forgiving choices in the genus for a first-time cycad grower. Give it room to spread, since a mature specimen eventually rivals large Cycas species in overall size.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in partial shade to full sun in deep, well-drained, humus-rich soil in zone 9b–11; this is one of the tallest-growing cycad species and needs long-term space overhead as well as at the base.

directions: Encephalartos transvenosus, the Modjadji cycad, is named for the famous stands of ancient specimens protected in the Modjadji Nature Reserve of Limpopo Province, South Africa, where centuries-old individuals form one of the largest cycad forests on Earth. It builds a tall, solitary, unbranched trunk crowned with long, gracefully arching, deep-green fronds, ultimately becoming one of the tallest species in the genus Encephalartos, far exceeding the squat, clumping habit of E. horridus or E. trispinosus. Growth is steady but slow even by cycad standards, so reaching significant trunk height in cultivation is a multi-generational project best appreciated as a long-term garden investment. Give it deep, well-drained soil and consistent moisture during the growing season to support its comparatively large frond mass.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun to light shade in well-drained soil in zone 9–11; this is one of the toughest and most adaptable Encephalartos species in cultivation, tolerating a wider range of soil and light than most of its relatives.

directions: Encephalartos altensteinii is native to coastal thicket and forest margins of the Eastern Cape and is historically notable as one of the first cycads ever grown in European collections, with a specimen brought to Kew Gardens in the 1770s still alive today. It develops multiple offset stems from the base over time, forming a broad, clustering multi-trunked clump rather than the single tall trunk seen in E. transvenosus, and its stiff, gently arching leaflets lack the extreme spination of E. horridus or E. ferox. It is among the most tolerant Encephalartos species of varied soil, light, and neglect, which is part of why it became a staple of botanical and estate gardens long before most other African cycads reached cultivation. Give young plants room, since a mature clump spreads considerably wider than any single trunk would suggest.
sources: Kew Science — Plants of the World Online: Encephalartos altensteinii

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun on lean, gritty, well-drained soil in zone 9–11; this compact, suckering species is well suited to smaller gardens where a full-size Encephalartos would be out of scale.

directions: Encephalartos trispinosus takes its name from the three sharp spines typically found at the tip of each stiff, blue-green leaflet, a distinctive detail that separates it at a glance from the smooth or variably spined leaflets of most other Encephalartos species. Native to rocky, dry valley scrub near the Fish River in the Eastern Cape, it stays low and freely suckers from the base to form a spreading clump of short stems rather than building any real trunk height. Its diminutive, clustering habit makes it noticeably smaller in scale than E. altensteinii or E. natalensis, fitting more easily into modest garden beds or large containers. Grow it in full sun with sharp drainage, and expect the clump to widen gradually over the years as new offsets emerge around the parent stems.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun on lean, gritty, well-drained soil in zone 9–11; this Eastern Cape highland species tolerates cooler winters better than lowland tropical cycads but still needs sharp drainage.

directions: Encephalartos princeps is native to the grassy, rocky hillsides around Cathcart and the Stormberg region of the Eastern Cape highlands, an unusually cool and seasonally dry habitat for a cycad. Its leaflets carry a soft silvery-blue sheen that is less intensely twisted and spined than the dramatic foliage of E. horridus, giving the whole crown a smoother, more refined silhouette. Coming from higher, cooler ground than most Encephalartos species, it copes with brief cold snaps somewhat better than lowland tropical relatives, though it still needs the same lean, fast-draining soil as its blue-leaved cousins. It is a long-standing favorite among cycad collectors for its color and moderate, manageable size.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated offset divisions in spring in partial shade to full sun in deep, well-drained, humus-rich soil in zone 9b–11; because only a single male clone exists in cultivation, this species can only be propagated vegetatively, never from seed.

directions: Encephalartos woodii has one of the most remarkable stories of any cultivated plant: a single multi-stemmed clump was discovered in 1895 in the Ngoye Forest of KwaZulu-Natal, all its stems were removed into cultivation over the following years, and no other wild individual — and critically, no female plant — has ever been found, leaving the species extinct in the wild and represented today only by genetically identical male clones propagated as offsets in botanical gardens worldwide. It forms a large, handsome trunk with long, gracefully arching, deep-green fronds, a scale and form broadly comparable to E. natalensis or E. transvenosus. Because every specimen in existence is a division of the same original plant, no viable seed can ever be produced, and all propagation depends entirely on basal offsets taken from established clumps. Growing one is largely a conservation and curiosity exercise, offered occasionally by specialist cycad nurseries and major botanical gardens rather than routine garden centers.
sources: Kew Science — Plants of the World Online: Encephalartos woodii
